The milestone comes from the canonical issue record, which is the one edge here that git does not hold, and `declared` says whether the project model has this id at all — a repository with no plan still gets the branches, and a typo still cannot read as work nobody did.

pages.title: trace.report
pages.description: Every issue at least one branch names with its branches and commits, every declared issue no branch names, and the newest stretch of the trunk with each commit attributed to the issue whose branches hold it or reported as unattributed. The tallies count both sides, so the proportion of the trunk that no execution contract accounts for is a number rather than an impression. Read from git on every call: the history changes outside this process.

pages.title: web.surfaces
pages.description: The web topology in route-precedence order, with each surface's mount, category, visibility, kind, producer, artifact, runtime feature and the provenance of every value a reader could be surprised by; and which ids are served, published and offered to a person. Answered from the resolution this process serves from, so it cannot disagree with what the router routes or what the home page lists.

pages.title: why.areas
pages.description: Every operational area the catalogue declares, each with the public moments that fall under it. Membership is derived from the moments and is never listed in an area's own file.

pages.title: why.audiences
pages.description: Every audience the catalogue declares, each with the public moments that name it. Membership is derived from the moments and is never listed in an audience's own file.

pages.title: why.diagnose
pages.description: What a reader's own symptoms imply: the moments the selection resolves to, the operational areas and audiences they weigh towards, and the capabilities, commands, claims, rules and use cases that answer them — each carrying the moments that produced it. Counting, not inference: there is no weighting and no percentage.

pages.title: why.list
pages.description: Every operational moment this repository holds, narrowed by any of the facets the catalogue itself reports, with the audiences, the areas, the derived filters and the counts. The default is the public catalogue; pass status=any for the drafts too.

pages.title: why.moment
pages.description: One operational moment in full: what it looks like, why it happens, what it costs, what this tool does about it, and every relation derived from its metadata — the responsibilities its claims belong to, the moments that name it, and the moments nearest it by shared area, audience and tag.

pages.title: why.validate
pages.description: Every finding over the catalogue: a reference that resolves to nothing, with the nearest candidate; a duplicate identity; a file name that disagrees with its id; and a public record that does not meet the floor its status promises. Errors make the catalogue invalid; warnings do not.

pages.title: worktree.inspect
pages.description: The canonical path of a branch, derived from its name alone, whether the branch exists, whether something occupies that path, the worktree holding the branch when one does, and what stands in the way of creating or migrating it. The answer for a branch that does not exist yet is the path `worktree create` would use.

pages.title: worktree.migration_plan
pages.description: One step per misplaced worktree with a branch: where it is, where it belongs, how it would move, the uncommitted work that moves with it, and what blocks it; plus the exceptions the migration cannot address by design — detached worktrees, stale registrations, the primary checkout off the trunk — each with what a person does about it. Planning changes nothing; `majordomus worktree migrate` applies it with a fingerprint taken before and after every move.

pages.title: worktree.status
pages.description: One worktree — the repository's own, or the one holding the directory the caller names — with its standing, its branch, its canonical path, its uncommitted work counted, whether it is where it belongs, and how many errors the whole topology carries. What an agent reads before it starts, and what the guard decides on.

pages.title: worktree.topology
pages.description: The repository, the container, the trunk and how it was decided, every registered worktree with its standing (primary, canonical, misplaced, detached, missing), its uncommitted work, its upstream distance and the issue its branch provably names, every local branch with or without a worktree and whether it is eligible for cleanup, every diagnostic with its code and remedy, and the tallies. Read from git on every call: the topology changes outside this process.

pages.title: Command line
pages.description: The native command line of the Rust executable, every command and argument, as clap declares it.

pages.title: The Rust executable
pages.description: The Rust executable of Majordomus.

pages.title: MCP surface
pages.description: The tools and resources the executable serves to an MCP client, the transports, the shared server, and what decides all of it.

pages.title: Modules
pages.description: The builtin modules of the executable: what each composes, where it stands, and where its source is.

pages.title: Generated artifacts
pages.description: What `majordomus generate` writes: every document with the encodings it is committed in — JSON for a program, YAML beside it, Markdown for a reader — each with its schema, its source and its hash, reconciled with the working tree. The declaration is the generator's own manifest; nothing here keeps a list.

pages.title: Capabilities
pages.description: The registry seen through itself: every capability with its kind, stability, provenance, exposures, benchmark and cache policy, and one capability in full.

pages.title: Command graph
pages.description: Every command this repository offers, from whichever program offers it: the Rust executable, the shell tool that carries the task lifecycle, and the workflows the repository declares for a person to run. Composed from the three declarations that already exist — the clap tree, the shipped command registry and the workflow runner's own dump — never from a list. Each command carries what running it changes, what it needs, where its argument values come from, and every surface that carries it, with the reason when one does not.

pages.title: Commit
pages.description: The commit as a value: the scope vocabulary this repository's own history yields, what the working tree would commit and how it divides, and the verdict on one message against the repository's commit policy.

pages.title: Continuity
pages.description: What this checkout's lifecycle is holding: the open episode, the record the next worker would resume from with the label that says how far to trust it, the newest progress note, and what is blocking acceptance. Read from the local half of the layer, which this process serves to the worker in front of it and never publishes.

pages.title: Deployment
pages.description: The deployments this repository declares, read from the canonical objects the index holds, and whether they would work — decided against the capability registry this process built and the workspace it sits in. Every operation is a read: a deployment is changed by the trusted command line and by CI, never over HTTP and never by an MCP client.

pages.title: Design system
pages.description: The one declaration of how every surface of this tool looks — the semantic roles, the status vocabulary, the type scale, the theme contract — as this executable carries it: its fingerprint, its tokens, what any one of them means, and whether the colours it pairs are readable on one another. The stylesheets the site and the Cockpit load, the tokens the executable's own pages compile in, and the dataset the site's templates read are all projections of it; a page compares its `--mj-design` with this fingerprint to know whether it is wearing the design this executable was built with.

pages.title: Development context
pages.description: The context a development session should be given, derived from the repository rather than composed by hand: given an issue, a milestone, an intent or a set of paths, the canonical objects that bear on the work, why each one is in the answer, what was left out and why, what collapsed into what, and the whole cost against a budget. The selection is structured — every entry keeps its identifier, its provenance, the selector that reached it and its confidence — because rendering a prompt is a projection of the selection and not the selection itself.

pages.title: Executable development scopes
pages.description: An issue and a milestone read as work to be done rather than as metadata: what a person authored, where the plan graph puts it, what happened to it locally, where its external projection stands, and whether a worker may start it — with the origin of every value on the value. Nothing here is a second project model: the records are the canonical ones, the status and the graph are `plan`'s, the branches and commits are `trace`'s, the readiness vocabulary refines three canonical statuses without replacing any, and the projection onto GitHub stays `scripts/github-sync`'s. Nothing here writes anything, which is what makes a user-authored GitHub value safe from it.

pages.title: Directory contracts
pages.description: The layer's directories as a hierarchy: the contract each one declares, what it owes and which contract said so, and the chain that applies to it once inheritance is resolved.

pages.title: Distribution
pages.description: How this project is packaged, published and installed: the platforms a release builds, the artifact names the one naming function derives, the installer's canonical command, the releases that were published, and what this build itself is. Every answer comes from share/distribution.yaml and the release records; no surface here states a fact of its own.

pages.title: Entities
pages.description: Every object of the layer as an addressable, cross-linked node: its route, its outgoing references, the references that resolve to it, the surfaces that answer for it, and what can be said about its enforcement without running anything. Nothing here enumerates kinds, entities or routes — an object of the index has a route because it is an object.

pages.title: Repository environment
pages.description: What this checkout is right now: the project and its version, the repository and its layer, version control, the toolchains it declares, what the layer holds, the workflows a person can run, the provider projections and the local services — one typed snapshot, with a provenance entry for every value in it. The direnv banner, the Cockpit's overview and this route are renderings of the same value.

pages.title: Evidence
pages.description: What actually ran, against which commit, and whether it still proves anything. The claims matrix binds a claim to a test by path; the ledger under .ai/repo/evidence records the latest execution of every test with the commit, the tree state, the digest of the test's own source, the time, the origin and the command that runs it again. Joining the two answers, per claim, whether the repository can honestly call it proven — and distinguishes a run recorded against this very commit from one whose inputs merely have not changed since, because collapsing those two is how a green badge stops meaning anything.

pages.title: Executions
pages.description: Running a capability of this registry as work that can be watched: started, followed event by event over the live channel, read back afterwards, and asked to stop. In memory; an execution does not outlive the process that accepted it.

pages.title: Completion gates
pages.description: Completion as a state the repository decides rather than a claim a worker makes: the validation gates this repository declares in its CI model, which of them a task's own change set selects, what each one last reported, whether that verdict still describes the tree it was taken over, and therefore whether the task may be called finished. A gate that has never reported is `queued` and not `pass`, a run whose files have changed since is `stale` and refuses exactly as a failure does, and a gate the change cannot affect is `exempt` rather than unknown.

pages.title: Graphs
pages.description: The graphs derived from the registry and the index: the executable's own capability registry, the shape of the layer, the rule dependencies, the decisions and what they put in force, and the use cases and what they exercise. Canonical nodes and edges; a rendering library is a consumer, never the shape.

pages.title: Health
pages.description: Whether what this process serves is healthy, decided by the engines that already decide it: the index's diagnostics, the registry builder, the benchmark projection's coverage, the comparison `generate --check` makes and the lease reading `server.status` answers from. No check here has an opinion of its own.

pages.title: Session lifecycle
pages.description: The episode lifecycle as an operator sees it: every open episode of this checkout's store rather than only the one the pointer follows, the episodes that can no longer close themselves, the commit this process is answering about against the commit the repository is on, what each provider's adapter declares it can do, and the tracked records a clone receives. Read from the local half of the layer and from the index; written by nothing here.

pages.title: Mesh
pages.description: The nodes this process discovered on the mesh: authenticated observations of other running Majordomus instances, converged into one registry, with the providers that heard them and the trust the policy assigned. Observation, never authority: a listed node can execute nothing here.

pages.title: Models
pages.description: The model catalogue the distribution declares — vendors, canonical model references, typed capabilities, context windows, lifecycle — and the explainable routing over it: what a stated need selects, what stands behind it, and why every excluded model fell out. Declared data; nothing here calls a model or reads a credential's value.

pages.title: Objects
pages.description: The declarative objects of the repository's AI layer: rules, prompts, profiles, policy, documents, milestones, issues, claims, and whatever kinds the repository adds; listed, read by URI, and searched.

pages.title: Obligations
pages.description: What a task owes before it may be called completed, and whether the evidence that discharged each obligation still describes this tree. The vocabulary is data the distribution ships and answers in any clone; the closure is read from the local half of the layer, which this process serves to the worker in front of it and never publishes. Read, never written: `majordomus evidence` records, and a second writer for one ledger would be a second account of the same events.

pages.title: Peers
pages.description: The workers of this repository, named by their own initialize, and what each announced it is working on — gathered from the board of every checkout, because a server serves a checkout and a repository worked on through linked worktrees has one board per worktree. In memory; gone with the processes.

pages.title: Performance
pages.description: This process's work counters and phase timings: what happened once at startup and what happens per call, for the structural tests and the benchmark evidence.

pages.title: The plan and its derivations
pages.description: The milestone and issue model of this repository, and everything derived from it that nobody authored: the status of each record, the dependency graphs above and below the milestone boundary, the topological execution waves, the roadmap order, the milestone being executed and the one issue to take next. Status is never stored — a record says what happened to it and the status follows from that and from the state of its dependencies — so no file can contradict the graph. This capability reads; writing a lifecycle marker into a record is `plan.transition`, which declares that it writes the repository.

pages.title: Product
pages.description: What this repository's product does for a person, as the features under the layer's features section declare it: each feature made of modules, commands, kinds, rules, documents, decisions, claims, use cases, Cockpit areas and web surfaces it names, with the interfaces it is exposed through, every count, the moments it answers and what is guaranteed derived from those references. The matrix of features against interfaces, the providers the tool has an adapter for, and the model's own validation. The homepage is a reader of this module and holds no inventory of its own.

pages.title: Public API quality
pages.description: What this executable's own public surface is held to, measured from its syntax tree: documentation that says more than the signature, an executable example on everything that carries behaviour, a module boundary something exercises, and every command of the command line accounted for against the capability registry. The rules are project.rust-public-api-quality and project.operation-transport-parity; this is the measurement of them.

pages.title: Recovery of the record stores
pages.description: The stray files a killed publish, an interrupted rename or an unfinished site build leave in the record stores, classified by reading the clock and the content, and swept exactly once. This is the capability that backs `majordomus recover` (ADR 0040): the command no longer decides what a stray is, it asks.

pages.title: Release
pages.description: What this project has shipped and what it would ship next, derived rather than maintained: the changelog composes the layer's release records, the decisions dated inside each release's window and the conventional commits in its range; the version report reads the two places the version is stated and says what the commits since the last release imply it should become.

pages.title: Repository
pages.description: The repository this process serves: its layer, its git state, the state of the index built from it, and its scope: what a worker reads of it and what it never reads.

pages.title: Rules
pages.description: What this repository refuses, and what it can actually show for each refusal. A rule declares a class — blocking, where a gate refuses the work, or advisory, where a reader is expected to have read it — and an enforcement block naming either the validator the dispatcher calls or the behavioural cases that prove it. This module joins that declaration to the tree and to the ledger of recorded runs, and reports, per rule, whether what it names is there, whether a runner owns it, whether it was ever run, whether the run passed, and whether the run is older than what it is about. A blocking rule whose proof is missing, dangling or failing is a finding, because a rule nobody can prove is a rule nobody enforces.

pages.title: Server
pages.description: The shared server of this checkout and of every other checkout of the same git repository: what each lease says, whether the server it names answers, whether what answers is the code on disk at this executable's version, and how many peers each one holds.

pages.title: The session domain
pages.description: The typed session domain: the lifecycle state machine an episode moves through, declared once in the executable and projected here rather than redrawn per surface, and the identities this checkout records — the repository, the checkout, the episode and the provider's own session — each with the canonical value and each store's own spelling of it, because the stores spell six things as three words and nothing said so.

pages.title: Traceability
pages.description: Which branches and commits realised an issue, and which issue and milestone a commit served — derived from git and from the canonical project model on every call, stored nowhere. A branch names an issue when one of its path components is an issue id; a commit belongs to the issue whose branches hold it; a commit no such branch holds is reported as unattributed rather than left out, because work with no execution contract is what a traceability report exists to make visible. Pull requests are a GitHub fact and this executable makes no network call: `scripts/traceability` reads them and joins them to this answer over the branch name.

pages.title: Web surfaces
pages.description: What this repository exposes over HTTP, resolved from the producers that make it rather than from a register anybody maintains: the routes the executable answers itself, the documentation build, and every generated report that declared its own mount. The same resolution serves the router, renders the home page and composes a publication.

pages.title: Why
pages.description: The operational failure modes this tool is a response to: the moments a reader recognises, the audiences that recognise them, the areas they fall under, and what a reader's own symptoms imply. Every entry is a file under the layer's why section; nothing here holds a list, and a moment added there is answered by all of these without a registration anywhere.

pages.title: Worktree topology
pages.description: Where every linked git worktree of this repository belongs and where each one is. The container is the primary checkout's sibling named with `-wt`, the path under it is the branch name with its hierarchy kept, and both are derived from git's own identity — the common directory, the registered worktrees, the branches — never from a registry, a configuration or the current directory. A worktree somewhere else is a typed diagnostic with a remedy; the migration that repairs it is a command-line operation of the same service.

pages.title: Rendering reference
pages.description: Representative Markdown for validating Flowbite Typography, syntax highlighting, tables, callouts and Mermaid across viewports. Not linked from navigation.

pages.title: Roadmap
pages.description: What comes after v0.1, in the order the milestone graph derives, each version gated by the previous one being accepted rather than by anyone's intention.

pages.title: Rules
pages.description: Every rule in force here — the vendored doctrine package and this repository's own — with the class it declares, the artefacts it names as its enforcement, whether the tree holds them, and the rules either side of it in the dependency graph.

pages.description: update generates CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, or any target you name, deterministically, and stamps each with the policy hash and the hash of its own content; a hand edit is detected and never silently overwritten

pages.title: Scope
pages.description: start takes the paths a task may touch; check and finish fail on files outside them; other worktrees' overlapping claims are reported

pages.title: State
pages.description: one active task per checkout in current.yaml, with branch, head, and working_tree computed from git, never authored

pages.title: Watch
pages.description: reports drift between policy, projections, state, scope, and git, each finding with the command that reproduces it

pages.title: Use cases
pages.description: What people do with it: a task, the commands that answer it, and what you are left holding, each one proved against the tool. Every step is a real invocation, every rule and promise a real object, and every example below was executed to make this page.

pages.title: Decide whether finished work is actually finished
pages.description: Evaluate a contract line by line instead of accepting a sentence that says the work is done.

pages.title: Add a use case and let the tool prove it
pages.description: Scaffold a draft for an uncovered command, validate it, run its scenario against the real tool, and see the coverage move.

pages.title: Adopt a repository that already has its own rules
pages.description: Install the supervisory layer into a repository with a hand-written CLAUDE.md, without the tool taking ownership of a file somebody else wrote.

pages.title: Getting started and adoption
pages.description: Bringing Majordomus into a repository, new or old, without losing what people already wrote.

pages.title: Block acceptance on a question nobody has answered
pages.description: Open a question against the task, watch finish refuse completion while it is unresolved, resolve it with the answer, and only then complete.

pages.title: Keep the prompts that started the work, below the model rather than around it
pages.description: Wire the provider hook, prove it by running a payload through it, and see that a prompt the tool could not parse is reported rather than silently dropped.

pages.title: Hand work over with a question still open, and keep it blocking
pages.description: Close a task into a handover while a question is unresolved, start the follow-up task, and see the same question still refuse acceptance there.

pages.title: Checkpoint long work so a stop costs minutes, not the day
pages.description: Record compact progress inside the active task at the profile interval, so a session that ends without warning leaves the next one a place to start.

pages.title: Decide what belongs in the AI context, as data
pages.description: Read the repository’s declared scope policy, see which paths are in and out of the index, and let doctor and the knowledge index apply it rather than a hardcoded list.

pages.title: Complete an issue only when its evidence exists
pages.description: See an issue refuse completion while a required piece of evidence is missing, read the roadmap the milestone state derives, and keep the GitHub projection a projection.

pages.title: Completion and quality gates
pages.description: Deciding whether work is finished, with a contract every line of which passes or fails.

pages.title: Sessions and handover
pages.description: Stopping and resuming work across sessions and workers from durable state, never a transcript.

pages.title: Use-case coverage
pages.description: Every public command, guaranteed claim and MCP tool against the use cases that name it, run it and carry evidence for it; the policy says which gaps fail.

pages.title: Deliver issues in waves the graph computes, and take the next one
pages.description: Validate the plan, read the execution waves the dependency graph yields, see which issues are ready and which are blocked on what, and take the one issue a worker should do now.

pages.title: Refuse a directory of the layer that documents nothing
pages.description: A directory added under the layer without a context document fails validation by name, nothing resolves against the tree until it says what it is for, and the same hierarchy is readable over MCP and the API without running the gate.

pages.title: Drift and reconciliation
pages.description: Detecting that policy, projections, state and git disagree, and putting them back in step.

pages.title: Extend what the executable serves by adding a file, never by rebuilding it
pages.description: Add a rule, a prompt or a knowledge node to .ai/ and have it appear as an MCP resource, an HTTP route and a reference entry, with the same binary.

pages.title: Extension
pages.description: Adding a kind, a rule, a command or a use case as data, with the checks that follow from it.

pages.title: Find an object of the layer without reading everything
pages.description: Search durable records literally across kinds from the shell, and ask the shared server the same question over MCP with majordomus_search and majordomus_get.

pages.title: Find out what has drifted since anyone last looked
pages.description: Ask what has moved, rather than whether anything is wrong.

pages.title: Follow a procedure the repository defines, and add another one
pages.description: Read the repository''s skills, take one as it is written, and add a new one by writing its file — no registry, no code, and a check that says what it examined.

pages.title: Gate CI on the tool itself, with an exit code that is a contract
pages.description: Run the checks CI runs, read every finding with the command that reproduces it, and rely on exit codes that mean one thing each: no code means warn and continue.

pages.title: Hand the repository to someone who cannot clone it
pages.description: Take a snapshot that a model can read or a gate can run in, without sending anything untracked and without losing the file modes on the way.

pages.title: Hand unfinished work to the next session
pages.description: Stop mid-task and leave the next worker something to act on that is not a transcript.

pages.title: Install the tool in one command, on a machine with no toolchain
pages.description: Paste one line, get a verified binary for this machine, and run majordomus init — no git, no Rust, no Node, no Python, no root, and no way to install an archive whose digest does not match.

pages.title: Record a decision so the next worker can find it
pages.description: Write down what was decided and why as state, then find it again without reading a conversation.

pages.title: Keep every provider bootstrap thin, generated and within budget
pages.description: Regenerate AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and the other provider files from one policy and prove they are stamped, point at the layer, stay under the line budget and resolve every reference.

pages.title: Know whether the work in this checkout is finished
pages.description: Ask the repository you are standing in, and be told what is still owed by name.

pages.title: Check the version before trusting a diagnosis
pages.description: Print the version every other surface derives from, and see the argument it refuses.

pages.title: Repository knowledge
pages.description: What the repository declares about itself: sources, nodes, edges, the plan, and searching them.

pages.title: Have the session opened and closed without anybody remembering to
pages.description: Wire the provider''s own session events, and the episode opens when the sitting begins, hands the worker what the last one left, records what a compaction is about to discard, and closes with a continuation record beside its envelope.

pages.title: Serving the layer to AI clients
pages.description: One shared server per repository, every client a peer, the same layer over MCP, HTTP and the command line.

pages.title: Move a repository from the pre-.ai layout to the layer
pages.description: See what a migration would move, move it with a backup, and prove the result is a layer the tool reads.

pages.title: Record what one worker did in one sitting
pages.description: Open a session, do the work under whatever tasks it touches, and close it into an envelope that references what it produced and copies nothing.

pages.title: Performance
pages.description: Benchmarks derived from the registry, baselines that are data, and budgets doctor reports against.

pages.title: Divide a working tree into commits, and hold every message to a policy
pages.description: Ask what this tree would commit and why, learn the scope vocabulary from the history rather than a table, and get a verdict on one message or on a whole range before a reviewer has to give one.

pages.title: Keep the plan as milestones and issues the tool can validate
pages.description: Declare milestones as outcomes and issues as execution contracts, and let the tool say what is ready and what is blocked.

pages.title: Policy and enforcement
pages.description: Declaring rules, proving they are wired, and reproducing a finding.

pages.title: Prove a rule is actually enforced, not merely written down
pages.description: Answer "is this rule real?" with a command rather than a reading of the source.

pages.title: Prove the tool is fast, not assume it, and refuse a regression
pages.description: Measure every public command and every capability of the executable against a committed baseline, and let the check fail on a regression rather than a reviewer noticing later.

pages.title: Prove what a task owed before calling it done
pages.description: A task declares what it owes, records evidence against each obligation, and is refused when that evidence no longer describes the tree it was taken over.

pages.title: Read back what happened, and keep the ledger within its cap
pages.description: Read the append-only ledger as operational history, filtered by task and event, validate every line, and rotate the oldest lines into an archive rather than deleting them.

pages.title: Read only the context that fits the budget, and know what was dropped
pages.description: Assemble the context a worker needs now in authority order, cut it to a line budget, and see every dropped section named with its reason.

pages.title: See which rules apply here and what enforces them
pages.description: List the effective rule set, read one rule as the tool reads it, and see which of them the tool enforces and from where.

pages.title: Record a decision as data, and prove the tool cannot accept it for you
pages.description: Read the decisions a repository holds, validate the whole set in one command, and watch the tool refuse to write the one status only a person may write.

pages.title: Close an episode whose client never came back
pages.description: A killed provider sends no end event. Close the episode it left open by evidence, exactly once, without claiming work it did not do.

pages.title: Start a session from a rendered framing, not a pasted transcript
pages.description: List the prompt assets the repository ships, render one against the durable state, and read the context it embeds.

pages.title: Resume in the right worktree, never against somebody else’s task
pages.description: Find the handover that belongs to this worktree and branch, and see a task record from another checkout reported as foreign rather than enforced here.

pages.title: Run several workers in one repository without them colliding
pages.description: Give each worker a declared scope, and find out immediately when two of them claim the same paths.

pages.title: Say what reached the remote and what did not
pages.description: The obligations that reach past the working tree are settled by asking git and the published site, so a report cannot call uncommitted work committed or unpushed work pushed.

pages.title: Say what your work is for, once, and have every surface say it
pages.description: Record an operational failure mode as one file and have the command line, the API, MCP and the website answer it without registering it anywhere.

pages.title: See what the repository holds, and run one of its capabilities, without reading a file
pages.description: Open the shared server in a browser and get the whole layer as pages: what exists, where each thing came from, what depends on what, what is failing, and a form that runs any capability.

pages.title: Serve the repository's AI layer to every AI client through one shared server
pages.description: Open the repository in any client the tool declares a provider for (docs/generated/providers.md) and have each of them read the same rules, prompts and knowledge over MCP from one process, seeing each other.

pages.title: Trace a change to the context documents it affects
pages.description: List the scoped context documents, resolve which apply to a path and why, and find out which documents a change set touches before it lands.

pages.title: Trust the policy and the profiles only after they are validated
pages.description: Prove that the canonical policy parses with every key it needs declared, that every profile parses and the default exists, and that what the policy declares as enforced is what actually runs.

pages.title: Work on a branch in the one worktree it belongs to
pages.description: Start a branch without choosing a path, find every checkout of the repository from any of them, and bring a stray one home with its uncommitted work intact.

pages.title: Parallel workers
pages.description: Several agents or people on one repository: claimed scopes, overlap, and who touched what.

pages.title: Why you need this
pages.description: 38 operational failure modes AI-heavy teams meet, who recognises each, what actually causes it, and what Majordomus does and does not do about it.

pages.title: A worktree nobody can decide to delete
pages.description: Isolation is cheap to create and expensive to reason about: nothing records what a worktree was for or whether its work landed.

pages.title: The interface changed and its contract document did not
pages.description: A contract maintained by hand beside the code it describes goes stale on the first change that forgets it.

pages.title: Operational areas
pages.description: The parts of running AI-assisted work these moments fall under, each with the ones that fall under it.

pages.title: Context and continuity
pages.description: What a worker knows when it starts, and what survives when it stops.

pages.title: Coordination and ownership
pages.description: Who holds what, who is doing what right now, and what happens where two workers meet.

pages.title: Model, effort and cost
pages.description: What was spent, on which task, at which capability, and whether the choice was ever recorded.

pages.title: Decisions
pages.description: What was settled, why, and whether the next worker can find out before reopening it.

pages.title: Documentation and drift
pages.description: Whether what is written still describes what exists, and how many copies of it there are.

pages.title: Rules and governance
pages.description: Which rules apply here, whether anything loads them, and whether they still agree with each other.

pages.title: Observability
pages.description: What actually happened while nobody was watching, in a form that is not a transcript.

pages.title: Verification and evidence
pages.description: Whether "done" is a claim or a fact, and what would prove the difference.

pages.title: Work and its state
pages.description: What is in flight, what is finished, and whether the repository agrees with the tracker.

pages.title: Who this is for
pages.description: The audiences that recognise these moments, each with the ones it recognises. Membership is declared by every moment and never listed here.

pages.title: Agency or consultancy
pages.description: Many clients, many repositories, and context that must transfer between people in hours rather than weeks.

pages.title: AI-native development team
pages.description: Several people and more assistants than people, working the same repository at the same time.

pages.title: Engineering lead
pages.description: Accountable for what shipped, without having watched any of it being written.

pages.title: Enterprise engineering
pages.description: Answerable to auditors, not only to users: what was done, by what, under which policy, with what evidence.

pages.title: Open-source maintainer
pages.description: Reviews contributions from people and machines they have never met, against conventions only they know.

pages.title: Platform and developer productivity team
pages.description: Owns the rules, the tooling and the execution environment that everybody else works inside.

pages.title: Research and experimental engineering
pages.description: Many more experiments than results, and the expensive part is remembering which ones were already tried.

pages.title: Solo builder
pages.description: One person, several assistants, and no one else to ask what was decided yesterday.

pages.title: A change that no plan ever asked for
pages.description: Work arrives with no bounded contract behind it, so its scope, its acceptance criteria and its ownership are all decided after the fact.

pages.title: The instruction file that grew into a rulebook
pages.description: Everything important gets appended to the always-loaded file, so every session pays for every rule and reads none of them carefully.

pages.title: A fluent contribution that could not have known the rules
pages.description: Assistants let anybody produce plausible contributions at volume; the conventions that make one correct are still only in the maintainers.

pages.title: The decision exists, in a conversation nobody can find
pages.description: A decision that was reached in a session is stored where only that session can read it, so it is neither reviewable nor discoverable.

pages.title: A hard-won discovery that never became knowledge
pages.description: A worker learns something expensive about the codebase, uses it once, and it dies with the session because nothing turned it into a durable record.

pages.title: The documented command that no longer works
pages.description: Examples are written once, in prose, and nothing ever executes them again.

pages.title: Accepting "done" because the model said so
pages.description: A fluent completion claim is accepted as evidence because nothing wrote down, beforehand, what would have to be true.

pages.title: A rule enforced by a hook that never runs
pages.description: Every artefact of enforcement exists — the rule, the script, the test — and no path connects them, so the control is fiction.

pages.title: A failure that was seen once and never again
pages.description: A failure observed inside a session is described in that session and nowhere else, so the next one starts from the report rather than the evidence.

pages.title: A capability the documentation promises and nothing proves
pages.description: A sentence describing what the software does is written once and never connected to anything that would fail if it stopped being true.

pages.title: The first hour in a repository nobody can explain quickly
pages.description: What is conventional in a codebase is knowledge held by its regulars, so every arrival — human or machine — pays for it again.

pages.title: Green tests over stale generated files
pages.description: Tests exercise the code and say nothing about the committed outputs derived from it, so the build is green and the artifacts are wrong.

pages.title: The map
pages.description: Every moment with who recognises it, the area it falls under, and the commands, capabilities, claims, rules and use cases that answer it — derived from the moments themselves.

pages.title: Code that quietly contradicts a written decision
pages.description: The decision was recorded and the implementation went the other way, because nothing relates a decision to the paths it governs.

pages.title: The issue says done and the repository disagrees
pages.description: Completion is recorded as a state change in a tracker rather than as evidence in the repository, so the two drift immediately.

pages.title: Nobody can reconstruct where the milestone actually is
pages.description: Progress is an aggregate that exists only in people, because the parts it aggregates were never recorded in a form anything can add up.

pages.title: Nobody can say why that worker was chosen
pages.description: Provider and model selection is made implicitly, per session, and recorded nowhere, so it cannot be reviewed or repeated.

pages.title: One worker undoing another worker's change
pages.description: A worker sees an unexplained change in its path, judges it wrong, and removes it — correctly, on the evidence it had.

pages.title: The policy changed and its four copies did not
pages.description: A decision is updated at its source and the generated copies keep serving the previous version, with nothing reporting the difference.

pages.title: Re-arguing a decision that was settled last week
pages.description: A decision whose reason lived in a conversation cannot be reviewed, only re-argued — by a worker with less information than the first one had.

pages.title: Re-explaining the same context to a brand-new session
pages.description: Repository knowledge that only ever existed in a conversation has to be re-transmitted by hand to every worker that follows.

pages.title: A result nobody can reproduce, including its author
pages.description: The result is recorded and the conditions that produced it are not, so it is an anecdote rather than a measurement.

pages.title: The rule for that directory, in a README no session ever loaded
pages.description: A local rule is either in the always-loaded file, where every session pays for it, or beside the code, where nothing relates it to the path being edited.

pages.title: The same dead end, explored twice
pages.description: Negative results are the majority of experimental output and the part nobody records, so the search space is re-explored.

pages.title: Two sessions in one checkout, standing on each other
pages.description: Two workers in one working tree see each other only as unexplained file changes, and each treats the other as noise.

pages.title: A public page promising something nothing tests
pages.description: Public material is written by a different act from the code, so it drifts ahead of the behaviour and nothing brings it back.

pages.title: Spend that cannot be tied to anything accepted
pages.description: Consumption is measured per account and outcomes are recorded per person, so the two can never be joined.

pages.title: The strongest model, at maximum effort, renaming a variable
pages.description: Capability, reasoning depth, context size and verbosity collapse into one habit — everything on — because nothing ever named them separately.

pages.title: A task "in progress" that nobody has touched for three weeks
pages.description: A status that was authored rather than computed is true at the moment of writing and decays silently from then on.

pages.title: Three copies of one explanation, and no way to tell which is current
pages.description: Every hand-maintained copy of a fact drifts on its own schedule, and a reader cannot tell which copy is the current one.

pages.title: Three roadmaps, and none of them true
pages.description: A plan kept in prose is a snapshot, and every copy of it drifts on its own schedule; stored status is an assertion that stays true after the world moves.

pages.title: Two agents fixing the same bug in two branches
pages.description: Two workers spend a day each on one defect because ownership was implicit and neither could see the other.

pages.title: Two different rulebooks for one repository
pages.description: Each provider reads its own hand-edited file, nothing relates them, and which contract applies depends on which tool is open.

pages.title: A cheap worker deciding something expensive
pages.description: Capability is dialled down for cost and nothing distinguishes the tasks where that is prudent from the ones where it is expensive.

pages.title: Asking what the workers did last night, and getting a transcript
pages.description: A conversation log records what was said, not what happened, so the operational question has to be answered by a person reading prose.

pages.title: A change whose provenance cannot be reconstructed
pages.description: Attribution stops at the commit, so what authorised a change, what verified it and what governed it are unrecoverable.

pages.title: Finished work that never reached the trunk
pages.description: Workers produce far more than integration absorbs, and nothing distinguishes work that is done from work that is done and landed.
